title: Continuous ultrametric functions extend across a component homeomorphism
statement: Let $Y,Z$ be topological spaces and $i:Y\to Z$ a continuous map. For a space $T$, let $q_T:T\to\pi_0(T)$ be its quotient by belonging to the same connected component (maximal connected subset), with the quotient topology. Suppose $h:\pi_0(Y)\to\pi_0(Z)$ is a homeomorphism with $h\circ q_Y=q_Z\circ i$. Let $A$ be a field [def-weil-field] with a multiplicative absolute value and metric $d(a,b)=|a-b|$, and assume $|a+b|\leq\max(|a|,|b|)$. Then $A$ is totally disconnected: every connected subset has at most one point. For $T=Y$ and $T=Z$, every continuous $f:T\to A$ has a unique continuous factor $\bar f:\pi_0(T)\to A$ with $f=\bar f\circ q_T$. Give $C(T,A)$ its pointwise ring operations. The actual precomposition map $i^*:C(Z,A)\to C(Y,A)$, $g\mapsto g\circ i$, is a ring isomorphism whose inverse is $E_i(f)=\bar f\circ h^{-1}\circ q_Z$. This holds for empty spaces and for the trivial absolute value, without completeness, local compactness or compactness of $Y,Z$.

proof.text: The identity $a-c=(a-b)+(b-c)$ gives $d(a,c)\leq\max(d(a,b),d(b,c))$. Apply [lem-sfb-ultrametric-space-totally-disconnected] to this genuine metric on $A$. It follows that every connected subset of $A$ has at most one point. The leaf requires neither completeness nor nontriviality of the absolute value.

source.place: Lemma 4.2.12, totally disconnected target hypothesis; agent absolute-value specialization of the general Mathlib ultrametric-space result.

proof.text: For each $T\in\{Y,Z\}$ apply [lem-sfb-continuous-connected-component-lift] with $B=A$. Step 1 verifies its only target hypothesis; $T$ is arbitrary. It gives the unique continuous factor $\bar f$ with $\bar f q_T=f$, and supplies continuity and surjectivity of $q_T$. These are precisely the quotient and factorization assertions required here.

source.place: Lemma 4.2.12, final proof paragraph; arbitrary-space form in Continuous.connectedComponentsLift and its continuity, composite and uniqueness theorems.

proof.text: The pointwise operations preserve continuity. Indeed addition satisfies $|(x\prime+y\prime)-(x+y)|\leq\max(|x\prime-x|,|y\prime-y|)$, negation is an isometry, and constants are continuous. For multiplication, put $M=1+|x|+|y|$ and choose $0<\delta<\min(1,\epsilon/M)$. If both input differences are $<\delta$, then $|x\prime|\leq\max(|x|,1)\leq M$ and $|x\prime y\prime-xy|\leq\max(|x\prime|\,|y\prime-y|,|y|\,|x\prime-x|)<\epsilon$. The pointwise ring laws are those of $A$. Thus $i^*(g)=g\circ i$ is a ring homomorphism: continuity follows by composition and preservation of $0,1,+,\cdot$ follows by evaluation at each point.

source.place: Agent elementary metric inequalities and pointwise ring calculation, supplementing Lemma 4.2.12.

proof.text: Define $E_i(f)=\bar f h^{-1}q_Z$; it is continuous by step 2 and continuity of $h^{-1}$. The equation $q_Zi=hq_Y$ gives $i^*E_i(f)=\bar f h^{-1}hq_Y=f$. If $g\in C(Z,A)$ and $f=g i$, then $(\bar g h)q_Y=\bar g q_Zi=g i=f$. Uniqueness in step 2 gives $\bar f=\bar g h$, whence $E_i(i^*g)=\bar g h h^{-1}q_Z=g$. Therefore $i^*$ is a bijective ring homomorphism and $E_i$ is its inverse. Its inverse preserves ring operations since applying the injective ring map $i^*$ to each required equality reduces it to that equality in $C(Y,A)$. No point was chosen: for empty $Y$ the homeomorphism forces empty $Z$, and both function rings have one element. The trivial absolute value gives a discrete genuine metric, so all preceding arguments still apply.
